body:
How coal forms

Coal is a combustible sedimentary rock rich in carbon. It forms mainly from the remains of ancient vegetation accumulated in swamps and other waterlogged environments. Burial beneath layers of sediment exposes this organic material to increasing pressure and temperature over long geological periods. It gradually loses moisture and volatile substances and becomes increasingly carbon-rich.

This slow transformation is called coalification or, in elementary textbooks, carbonisation. The coal produced depends on the original organic matter and the geological conditions of burial and alteration. Coal, petroleum and natural gas are fossil fuels, but coal predominantly originates from ancient terrestrial vegetation, while petroleum commonly forms from organic matter deposited in sedimentary basins, often in marine environments.

Ranks of coal

The rank of coal describes the degree of coalification. Greater coalification generally corresponds to a higher carbon proportion and lower inherent moisture, although the heating value of an individual coal sample also depends on its mineral matter and other properties.

Material or coal rankMain characteristicsImportant association
PeatPartly decomposed plant matter; very high moistureEarly stage or precursor of coal formation
LigniteBrown, relatively soft and moisture-richLower-rank coal; used in nearby power and industrial plants
Bituminous coalMore coalified, relatively high carbon contentCommonly used for electricity, industry and certain metallurgical applications
AnthraciteHard, highly coalified and relatively low in volatile matterHighest conventional coal rank

Peat is often shown at the beginning of the coal-formation sequence, but it is also treated as a precursor rather than fully developed coal in geological classification. Lignite is often called brown coal. Anthracite is the highest conventional rank; this does not mean it is the most common coal mined in India.

Coal rank is different from commercial grade

Coal sold for industrial use is also classified by its fuel properties. India's Ministry of Coal grades non-coking coal mainly according to gross calorific value (GCV), the amount of heat released when a specified mass of fuel burns completely under defined testing conditions.

The non-coking coal grading system includes G1 to G17. G1 represents coal with GCV exceeding 7,000 kcal/kg, whereas G17 covers GCV exceeding 2,200 and not exceeding 2,500 kcal/kg. A smaller numerical grade label therefore corresponds to a higher GCV band in this system.

Coking coal is classified differently, with ash content playing an important role in its grades. Coal rank, GCV grade and coking suitability must not be treated as equivalent labels.

Coking and non-coking coal

Coking coal is coal that softens and forms a coherent, porous mass when heated without air under suitable conditions. It is used to produce metallurgical coke, an important material in blast-furnace ironmaking. Non-coking coal is generally used as fuel in power stations, cement production and other industries.

Not every bituminous coal is suitable for coking. Coking ability depends on specific properties, not simply on carbon percentage. Anthracite is high-rank coal but is not automatically suitable for metallurgical coke production.

Products obtained from coal processing

When suitable coal is heated strongly in the absence of air, it undergoes destructive distillation, yielding:

  • Coke: a tough, porous material containing a very high proportion of carbon; important in iron and steel production.
  • Coal tar: a complex dark liquid containing many organic substances used as chemical raw materials.
  • Coal gas: a combustible gaseous mixture produced during coal processing.

These products are not identical to the products obtained by refining crude petroleum. In particular, coal tar and petroleum-derived bitumen have different origins, although both have historically been used in industrial applications.

Prelims focus

  • Coal forms mainly from buried vegetation through coalification.
  • Lignite is brown, moisture-rich, lower-rank coal.
  • Anthracite is the highest conventional coal rank.
  • Non-coking coal grades G1–G17 are based on gross calorific value.
  • Coking suitability is important for metallurgical coke production.
  • Trap: Anthracite, the highest coal rank, is not synonymous with coking coal.

[Sources: NCERT, Science, Class 8, chapter 5, Coal and Petroleum, printed pp. 56–58; NCERT, Contemporary India II, Class 10 Geography, chapter 5, Minerals and Energy Resources, section Coal; NCERT, India: People and Economy, Class 12 Geography, chapter 7, Mineral and Energy Resources, section Coal, printed pp. 78–80; Ministry of Coal, Coal Grades, GCV and coking-coal classification, coal.nic.in, page updated 6 October 2026; consulted 15 November 2026.]

pictures.caption: Coalification generally increases carbon concentration while reducing moisture and volatile matter.

title: Coal: Formation, Ranks, Grades and Industrial Products

body:
Coal resources are unevenly distributed

India's coal resources are concentrated in particular sedimentary formations and river valleys. Their location helps explain the development of coal-based power stations and heavy industries in eastern and central India.

The major geological groups are Gondwana coal and Tertiary coal. Gondwana deposits are older and account for most of India's major coal resources. The Damodar, Son, Mahanadi and Godavari river systems are associated with important coal-bearing areas. Younger Tertiary coal occurs notably in parts of northeastern India.

Important coalfields and their states

Coalfield or areaState or statesKey association
JhariaJharkhandDamodar Valley; important coking-coal region
BokaroJharkhandDamodar Valley
RaniganjWest BengalDamodar Valley
TalcherOdishaMahanadi coal-bearing region
KorbaChhattisgarhMajor coal and thermal-power centre
SingrauliMadhya Pradesh and Uttar PradeshCoal mining and thermal-power region
Singareni coalfieldsTelanganaGodavari Valley coal
Wardha ValleyMaharashtraCoal-bearing region

Jharia is in Jharkhand, while Raniganj is in West Bengal. Both belong to the wider Damodar Valley coal region. Singrauli extends across Madhya Pradesh and Uttar Pradesh, so associating it exclusively with one state can be misleading.

Tertiary coal and lignite

Tertiary coal deposits occur in northeastern areas including Assam, Meghalaya, Arunachal Pradesh and Nagaland. These are different from the extensive Gondwana coalfields of eastern and central India.

Lignite is important in Neyveli, Tamil Nadu, and also occurs in Rajasthan and Gujarat. Because lignite generally contains substantial moisture, transporting it over long distances can be less economical than using it near the mine. This helps explain the association of some lignite deposits with nearby power and industrial facilities.

Gujarat's lignite resources

Gujarat has lignite deposits and mining activity in Kutch, Bharuch, Surat and Bhavnagar. Important associated locations include Mata-no-Madh and Umarsar in Kutch, Tadkeshwar in Surat district and the Bhavnagar lignite belt. These locations are associated with the Gujarat Mineral Development Corporation and other mining operators.

Gujarat's lignite resources should not be confused with the large Gondwana coalfields of Jharkhand, Odisha or Chhattisgarh. Gujarat also receives coal from other parts of India and from overseas for particular industrial and power requirements.

Methods of coal extraction

Open-cast mining removes the overlying soil and rock, called overburden, to reach a deposit relatively close to the surface. Large excavators and haulage equipment are used. This method can support large-scale production but disturbs the surface landscape and requires land reclamation.

Underground mining reaches deeper deposits through shafts or other underground openings. It involves additional concerns such as ventilation, methane accumulation, roof stability, mine fires and water ingress. The method chosen depends on geological depth, deposit characteristics, safety and operating conditions.

From mine to consumer

Coal extracted from a mine is often called run-of-mine coal. It may need crushing, sizing or washing before use. Coal washing removes some mineral impurities and reduces ash content in the usable product, but it also generates rejects that require management.

Coal is transported through combinations of railways, roads, conveyors and coastal shipping. Railway freight is especially important for moving large coal quantities to distant power stations. A power station located close to a coalfield is called a pithead power station; it can reduce the distance over which bulky coal must be transported.

Coal availability at a mine and coal availability at a power station are not identical. Production may be sufficient in aggregate while rail capacity, adverse weather, stock management or the quality of coal causes shortages at particular consumers.

Prelims focus

  • Jharia and Bokaro are in Jharkhand; Raniganj is in West Bengal.
  • Talcher is associated with Odisha, Korba with Chhattisgarh and Singareni with Telangana.
  • Singrauli extends across Madhya Pradesh and Uttar Pradesh.
  • Neyveli in Tamil Nadu is associated with lignite.
  • Gujarat's lignite regions include Kutch, Surat, Bharuch and Bhavnagar.
  • Trap: A pithead power plant is located near a coal mine; it is not a distinct method of generating electricity.

[Sources: NCERT, India: People and Economy, Class 12 Geography, chapter 7, Mineral and Energy Resources, sections Coal and Distribution of Minerals, printed pp. 74–80; NCERT, Resources and Development, Class 8 Geography, chapter 3, Mineral and Power Resources, printed pp. 24–32; Gujarat Mineral Development Corporation, 62nd Annual Report 2024–25, Plant Locations and Lignite Projects; Coal Controller's Organization, Lignite Mine Statistics, coalcontroller.gov.in; consulted 15 November 2026.]

pictures.caption: Open-cast lignite extraction is an important part of Gujarat's mineral-energy economy.

body:
Electricity from the heat of coal

A coal-based thermal power station converts the chemical energy stored in coal into heat and then into mechanical and electrical energy. The main working principle is the production of steam to rotate a turbine connected to an electric generator.

The word thermal means related to heat. Coal, oil and natural gas can all be used in thermal generation. Therefore, a statement about total thermal electricity generation must not automatically be interpreted as a statement about coal alone.

The basic steam-power cycle

  1. Fuel preparation and combustion: Coal is prepared for the boiler, commonly by crushing and pulverising it. It burns in the presence of oxygen and releases heat.
  2. Steam generation: Heat from combustion converts water into high-temperature, high-pressure steam in the boiler system.
  3. Turbine rotation: The steam expands through a turbine, causing its blades and shaft to rotate.
  4. Electricity generation: The turbine drives an electric generator, which converts mechanical energy into electrical energy.
  5. Condensation: Steam leaving the turbine is cooled in a condenser and converted back into water.
  6. Water circulation: The condensed water is pumped back towards the boiler, allowing the water-steam cycle to continue.

This is the elementary operating principle of a steam thermal power plant. A cooling tower, where provided, helps reject unwanted heat to the environment through the cooling-water system. It is not the component that generates electricity.

Combustion and the conditions for burning

Combustion is a chemical reaction in which a fuel reacts with oxygen and releases heat. Coal contains carbon and other combustible substances. During complete combustion of carbon, carbon dioxide forms. Inadequate oxygen or poor mixing can lead to incomplete combustion and the production of carbon monoxide or unburned material.

Combustion requires a combustible material, sufficient oxygen and conditions allowing the fuel to reach its ignition temperature. The ignition temperature is the minimum temperature at which a substance catches fire under specified conditions.

Thermal efficiency

Thermal efficiency is the proportion of the fuel's heat input converted into useful electrical energy. It indicates the effectiveness of energy conversion, not how frequently the plant operates.

For an elementary example, suppose a power station receives 100 MJ of chemical energy from coal and delivers 35 MJ of electrical energy. Its thermal efficiency is 35%. The remaining 65 MJ is not converted into useful electricity; much of it is rejected as heat, while other losses occur in the plant.

The efficiency of an actual station depends on boiler and steam conditions, fuel quality, equipment condition and operating load. Supercritical and ultra-supercritical steam plants use higher steam conditions than conventional subcritical plants and can achieve better efficiency. Higher efficiency generally reduces the amount of coal required per unit of electricity, although it does not eliminate fossil-fuel emissions.

Installed capacity, generation and plant load factor

Installed capacity is the rated power of the generating equipment. Electricity generation is the energy produced over a period. Plant load factor (PLF) compares actual generation during a period with the generation possible if the plant operated at its rated capacity continuously throughout that period.

Consider a 100 MW power station. At full output for 8,760 hours, its theoretical annual generation would be 876 million kWh. If it actually generates 600 million kWh, its annual PLF is approximately 68.5%. A lower PLF can result from maintenance, breakdowns, fuel shortages or lower demand; it does not directly reveal the plant's thermal efficiency.

Other important plant considerations

Coal quality affects performance. High ash content adds non-combustible material that must be heated, moved and disposed of. High moisture reduces useful heat available from the fuel. Coal preparation, reliable supply, adequate cooling water and appropriate maintenance are important for continuous operation.

The generated electricity is transmitted through the power network to consumers. Before delivery, some electrical energy is consumed by the station's own equipment and some is lost in transmission and distribution. Gross generation, net generation and electricity reaching consumers are therefore different quantities.

Prelims focus

  • Coal's chemical energy becomes heat, then turbine motion and finally electricity.
  • The boiler produces steam; the turbine rotates; the generator produces electricity.
  • The condenser converts exhaust steam back into water.
  • Thermal efficiency measures useful electrical output relative to heat input.
  • Plant load factor measures actual generation relative to potential generation at rated capacity.
  • Trap: A cooling tower removes heat; it is not the source of electrical generation.

[Sources: NCERT, Science, Class 8, chapter 6, Combustion and Flame, sections 6.1–6.2; NCERT, Science, Class 10, chapter Sources of Energy, section Thermal Power Plant; NCERT, Indian Economic Development, Class 11, chapter 8, Infrastructure, section Power/Electricity.]

pictures.alt: Coal heats a boiler; steam drives a turbine and generator, then condenses into water. A pump returns water, while cooling equipment rejects heat.
pictures.caption: Coal produces heat, steam drives the turbine, and the generator produces electricity.

pictures.alt: Thermal efficiency compares 35 MJ with 100 MJ of fuel heat; PLF compares 600 with 876 million kWh of possible annual generation.
